versions.note: Version 1: the book as first published in review mode. Text at 7f6775b2 (the Whittick 1984 rows W1-W3, with the owner's approved W1/W2 wording, joined to Parts 1 and 5); render of 2026-09-16 06:52, so the Whittick paragraphs are in the text but not yet in the PDF until the owner's next export.

Version 2 (25 September 2026). The book takes up the suggestion of immunity: chapter 4.6 now closes with the United States' 2016 suggestion for Israel's former Minister of Defense in Doğan v. Barak, read against the three bars of 1607, and chapter 3.2 § B with the Eleventh Amendment as the honest route beside the foreign line's removal by comity, statute and an Executive letter. Every quotation and citation in the book has been checked against the shelf before this release: two quotations were conformed to their sources (the 1641 Act's 'Courts holden before the President and Councell in the Marches of Wales'; Federalist No. 70's 'vigorous executive'), the two control counts in note ii7g were rounded, pins into the Suggestion of Immunity now follow the ECF stamp, and the bibliography gains fifteen rows (Chisholm, Ex parte McCardle, Ex parte Bradley, Samantar, the Schooner Exchange among them). Text at 793fbae2; the PDF is the 16 September export until the author's next.

Version 3 (25 September 2026). Three decisions the notes cite only inside 'quoting' parentheticals now stand in the bibliography: Miller v. Fenton, 474 U.S. 104 (1985), Brinegar v. United States, 338 U.S. 160 (1949), and Riley v. California, 573 U.S. 373 (2014), each read at its first page and at the page the quoting court took its words from (114, 171 and 381) in the Library of Congress print. No sentence of the body changes; the sources register is at its eleventh build. Text at 5cfe4e2a; the PDF is the 16 September export until the author's next.

Version 4 (25 September 2026). Chapter 4.6 now closes on two propositions about the suggestion of immunity. The first is the relation: every immunity this book traces sits inside the bond of sovereign and subject, while the suggestion is the forum sovereign refusing its own subject on a stranger's behalf, on a consent Marshall said the nation implies and may withdraw. The second is the record: the judgment is what the third bar denies, nominal damages redress a completed violation, and the sequence from Filártiga to the Torture Victim Protection Act, from Sabbatino to the act-of-state amendment, and from the Iran judgments to the asset statute shows the political branches acting on records, as Federalist No. 80 said they should. Nine works join the bibliography. Text at 99661cff; the PDF is the 16 September export until the author's next.

Version 6 (2026-09-25): 4.6 gains the USS Liberty paragraph (the 1967 claims espoused and paid to the Government; Dames & Moore's name for the practice; the Court of Inquiry counsel's 2004 affidavit stated as an officer's sworn account and no more; the House Record of June 8, 2026) with the servicemen sentences, and a closing paragraph on the premise the suggestion rests on: Marshall's implied consent of 1812, "less determinate, exposed more to the uncertainties of construction," never since put to proof, set against Hilton's comity and reciprocity, Sabbatino's agreement condition and the Act's implied waiver, and answered for Israel from the record (the 1951 treaty's Article V opening each party's courts to the other's nationals; the Civil Wrongs (Liability of the State) Law treating the State like any incorporated body, with thousands of such claims tried; the 2008 immunity statute drawn on our lines). 3.2 gains § D, Article I, Section 8: the record Congress needs and the branch that holds it (Article III's foreign States clause; the Section 8 clauses and the Statement and Account; McGrain, Watkins, Reynolds, Richardson; treason's enemy element, Cramer, the Prize Cases, Federalist 43; court, reprisal and war; Dames & Moore on practice), with one sentence on how an ally is made in the open (the 1951 treaty; 22 U.S.C. § 2321k(b); the 2014 Act). Notes si17–si25, cs1–cs8. Bibliography +19 rows since version 4, 6 amended. Register v14. Version 5 was prepared for the Liberty and § D text alone and never published; this entry supersedes it.

Version 7 (2026-09-25): two chapter 4.6 paragraphs broken at their own joints on the owner's Word comments, with no wording changed. The paragraph that relabels the three bars of 1607 becomes four: the bars; the lineage from Marshall's 1812 exemption through the servant's status in 1895 to the citation of 2016; the first respect, the relation between sovereign and subject that the foreign case lacks; the forum's own act, the Restatement clause, Ex parte Young and the second respect, the repair. The Liberty paragraph becomes four: the attack and the espousal; the Court of Inquiry and the Record of June 8, 2026; the servicemen; what the book holds and the three dates, 1967, 2016 and the reform of 1976 between them.

Version 8 (2026-09-25): the fourth Liberty paragraph of chapter 4.6 now ends by naming the three parties in their places, the Department of State that receives and decides the plea, the United States as the sovereign whose citizen was killed and whose court stays closed, and Israel as the accused, and by saying that the one thing that changed between 1967 and 2016 was the law, changed back by a letter. The framing text is brought level with the week's additions: the Part 3 abstract carries the argument of chapter 3.2 § D; the Introduction's map of the Parts names it; the Part 4 abstract names chapter 4.6's reading of the letter of 2016 beside the Liberty claims of 1967; the Conclusion to Parts 2 and 3 says where the transfer runs when the wrong is a foreign state's; and the Conclusion states what chapter 4.6 adds, the one case in which the rule's reserved forum still operates in America and the presumption of 1812 on which it rests.
